analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new offshore oil and gas drilling off Florida's Gulf and Atlantic coasts.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Florida-delegation bill to permanently ban offshore drilling off the state's coasts was referred to the House Resources Committee in April 2001 and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a permanent ban into law against new oil and gas leasing in the eastern Gulf of Mexico, the Straits of Florida, and the South Atlantic waters along Florida's coast. It would also require a full environmental review and the state's sign-off before any lease options are sold, and it would authorize about $90 million to buy back existing oil and gas leases near Florida's coast. It was introduced by Rep. Joe Scarborough with cosponsors from both parties in the Florida delegation, was sent to the House Resources Committee, and died there without ever reaching the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Florida's coastal residents, beach communities, tourism businesses, and commercial and recreational fisheries would gain permanent protection from oil spills, drilling rigs off their shores, and the industrial activity that comes with offshore development. Taxpayers generally benefit from cleaner coasts, and the state gains a veto-like role over drilling decisions through the required consistency certification.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Florida's coastal communities and tourism economy

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a section to the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act barring the Interior Secretary from issuing any lease for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the eastern Gulf of Mexico, the Straits of Florida, and the South Atlantic planning area down to the Florida-Georgia border.

It requires an environmental impact statement under the National Environmental Policy Act, plus a certification from the affected state under the Coastal Zone Management Act, before an option to lease can be sold — giving Florida a formal say over drilling near its shores.

It authorizes the Interior Secretary to buy back dozens of existing oil and gas leases near Florida — in the Destin Dome, Desoto Canyon, Pensacola, Apalachicola, and other Gulf planning areas — at a total authorized cost of $90,162,402, permanently removing those areas from development.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose access to new drilling areas off Florida, though the bill would pay leaseholders roughly $90 million in federal money for the existing leases it retires. Federal taxpayers bear that buyback cost, and the nation forgoes whatever oil and gas those areas would have produced.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies; taxpayers fund the buyback

drawbacks.text: The buyback authorizes $90,162,402 in federal spending to retire existing leases, a direct cost to taxpayers that compensates energy companies for lease rights they already hold.
The environmental review requirement contains a carve-out: it does not apply to plans for the production and transportation of natural gas, weakening the review for that category of activity.
Energy industry supporters argue permanently withdrawing large offshore areas reduces domestic oil and gas supply, with effects on energy prices and federal leasing revenue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection — a permanent statutory ban on drilling off Florida's coasts — directly serves the people who live on, work on, and visit those coasts, and the $90 million lease buyback is a modest one-time cost compared with the value of the tourism and fishing economies it shields. The natural gas carve-out is a real gap, and the loss of domestic energy supply is a legitimate trade-off, but on balance the bill's costs fall on one industry while its benefits are broad.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing or floor vote until the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Scarborough (R-FL) introduced the bill on April 26, 2001, with cosponsors from both parties in the Florida delegation.

It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Resources, and on May 3, 2001, was referred to that committee's Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, with an executive comment requested from the Interior Department.
No further action is recorded: the bill never received a subcommittee or committee vote and never reached the House floor before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies retained their existing leases and the possibility of new federal leasing in the eastern Gulf, and the Interior Department kept full discretion over drilling decisions off Florida. Florida's coastal communities got nothing from the bill they had bipartisan support for.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies and drilling-friendly officials

for.name: Rep. Joe Scarborough
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban offshore drilling off Florida and referred it to the House Resources Committee.

for.name: 14 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support — 8 of 208 House Democrats and 6 of 223 House Republicans — a bipartisan, all-Florida roster.

against.name: House Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over offshore leasing
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; after referring it to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on May 3, 2001, no further action was taken before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan and regional: the bill was introduced by a Republican and drew 8 Democratic and 6 Republican cosponsors, all from the Florida delegation, while opposition to moving it never had to take a recorded position because no vote was ever scheduled.

industries.note: The bill bars them permanently from new leasing in the eastern Gulf, the Straits of Florida, and the South Atlantic off Florida, though it would pay $90 million to buy back the specific existing leases listed in the text. Drilling near Florida's coast carries spill and industrial risks that fall on coastal residents, so the industry's interest in these waters runs against the people living there.

Beach tourism depends on clean, rig-free coastlines; a permanent drilling ban protects the beaches, fishing charters, and coastal economies that draw visitors. The industry's interest and the public's interest in unspoiled coasts line up.
The bill is scoped to protect marine and coastal resources and fisheries in the covered planning areas by keeping drilling platforms and spill risk out of fishing grounds off Florida.
